pr_body:
Introduces 2 new functions to use the default `.env` parser. 

## `process.loadEnvFile(path)`

- In order to load the `.env` file in the current directory:

```js
process.loadEnvFile()
```

- Load a specific path:

```js
process.loadEnvFile('./development.env')
```

## `util.parseEnv(content)`

- In order to parse an existing string:

```js
assert.deepStrictEqual(require('node:util').parseEnv('HELLO=world'), { HELLO: 'world' });
```

Fixes https://github.com/nodejs/node/issues/51413
Ref https://github.com/nodejs/node/issues/49148


------

Thank you [Sentry](https://sentry.io) for sponsoring this work!

We can look at this another way: what’s the one thing that the user can’t already do today? We already have APIs for loading files. We already have an API for setting environment variables (`process.env = { ...process.env, moreEnv }`). What we don’t have is a way to parse an `.env` file _in the way that Node does._ Sure there’s `dotenv`, but it supports more features than `--env-file` does. If the user wants to parse a `.env` file in exactly the same way that Node does, that’s an API that only Node can provide, and that doesn’t currently exist.

But this PR doesn’t add such an API, unless you intend to get its input from a file _and_ you intend to immediately set its output on `process.env`. We’ve already mentioned some potential non-file locations for getting `.env` file input (a secrets service like Vault or AWS Secrets Manager, a file that needs decryption, a network call) and an example of a destination other than `process.env` is defining the environment variables to be passed into a child process, like `exec(someCommand, { env: parseEnv(someEnvFileContents) })`. This is the downside of a single API that merges together a multistep process (loading a file, parsing it, setting the variables): there are use cases that just aren’t possible, or we need to add options to the API to break it apart to make these use cases possible.

I agree that the vast majority of users probably just want to load a `.env` file from disk and immediately set it on `process.env`. So to handle the other use cases, either we need to add an options object with an ever-growing set of options, or create multiple APIs. How about:

1. `process.loadEnvFile(filePathOrURLInstance)`: Reads the path from disk (erroring if not present; use try/catch to handle nonexistent paths), parses it, and sets it on `process.env`.
2. `util.parseEnv(envFileContents)`: Takes `.env` file contents passed in as a string and parses into an object.

With two APIs, neither one needs an options object, at least for all of the use cases I’ve thought of so far. The common case remains the one-liner `process.loadEnvFile(new URL('.env', import.meta.url))` and uncommon cases can be strung together, like:

```js
import { exec } from 'node:child_process'
import { readFile } from 'node:fs/promises'
import { parseEnv } from 'node:util'

const envFileContentsEncrypted = await readFile(new URL('.env.encrypted', import.meta.url), 'utf8')
const envFileContents = btoa(envFileContentsEncrypted) // Not real, I know
const envVariables = parseEnv(envFileContents)
exec('echo $ENV_VAR', { env: envVariables })
```
@mcollina Would you be ok with @GeoffreyBooth's suggestion of an util that takes the text of the file instead of the path? It would allow the users to do more things.
I hope I addressed all the comments. Appreciate it if you could re-review it. cc @mcollina @RafaelGSS @targos @GeoffreyBooth @aduh95
Sorry for not reviewing everything at once, it's a relatively big PR and I didn't remember all the edge cases in the first iteration.

issue_context.title: Add a feature to parse .env file by default
issue_context.body:
### What is the problem this feature will solve?

As of now current NodeJS requres to explicitly specify path to .env file whereas [dotenv](https://www.npmjs.com/package/dotenv) makes it by default. Users have to run scripts starting  with `node` keyword to explicitly specify .env file path. Whereas `npm` or `npx` commands do not support `--env-file` flag to pass it to node. For users who wants to exclude useage of  external [dotenv](https://www.npmjs.com/package/dotenv) it seems inconvenient.

### What is the feature you are proposing to solve the problem?

In order to get rid of [dotenv](https://www.npmjs.com/package/dotenv) library I propose to parse `.env` file if it exests in project root folder. 

### What alternatives have you considered?

Switching back to [dotenv](https://www.npmjs.com/package/dotenv)
comments:
> I propose to parse `.env` file if it exests in project root folder.

This would of course introduce a security issue bad enough that we will probably never have this behavior as default. However there might be other ways to solve the problem at hand.

> Whereas `npm` or `npx` commands do not support `--env-file` flag to pass it to node.

Can you give a specific example where this is a problem, ideally in the form "expected behavior vs actual behavior".

@aduh95 
With dotenv I just call `require('dotenv').config()` to programmatically set environment variables from a .env file. I run a cli tool in such a way `npx myclitool`.
In current Node there is no way to do it from the code, the only way is cli `--env-file` argument. To set a variables using NodeJs I have to modify my script like that `node node_modules/@dependency/cli/bin/myclitool.js --env-file=.env`
To sum up: it would be enough to have **Programmatic API** as requested in feature implementation [comment](https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/48890#issuecomment-1646746252). Probably the issue should be renamed respectively.

~Note that you can also use the `NODE_OPTIONS` env variable~ (`NODE_OPTIONS='--env-file=.env' npx myclitool`). EDIT: that was wrong, sorry, I forgot `--env-file` is not allowed in `NODE_OPTIONS`

/cc @anonrig

Please do not do this. We have projects that make use of an `.env` file for consumption by another application, not directly related to Node.js, but those projects use Node.js tooling. If Node.js started automatically parsing the `.env` which is not meant for it, suddenly it would be using variables that it previously didn't, which would break the current behavior in a few cases.
I'll open a PR for adding a function similar to dotenv.config()
